title: Counterpoint
intro: Counterpoint is the craft of combining melodies that are independent yet sound good together. Species counterpoint, codified by Fux in 1725, teaches it in five steps of increasing rhythmic freedom against a fixed melody, the cantus firmus.

blocks.text: Harmony looks at music vertically, chord by chord; counterpoint looks horizontally, line by line. Bach's fugues, Palestrina's masses and the inner voices of any good arrangement are counterpoint. Its rules are the source of the voice-leading rules in Voice Leading (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/voice-leading).

items: Contrary motion: one voice up, the other down. The most independent.
Oblique motion: one voice holds while the other moves.
Similar motion: both move the same way by different intervals.
Parallel motion: both move the same way by the same interval. Parallel thirds and sixths are fine; parallel perfect fifths and octaves are forbidden because the voices fuse.

blocks.text: One note of counterpoint against each note of the cantus firmus, all consonances. The rules (after Fux and Jeppesen):

items: Begin and end on a perfect consonance (unison, fifth or octave); the counterpoint below the cantus must begin on the unison or octave so the tonic is in the bass.
Use only consonances: unison, thirds, fifths, sixths, octaves (and their compounds). No fourths, seconds or sevenths, no augmented or diminished intervals.
No parallel fifths or octaves; approach perfect consonances by contrary or oblique motion.
Prefer imperfect consonances (thirds and sixths) in the middle; no more than three in a row of the same kind.
Mostly stepwise motion; leaps are fine if followed by a step in the opposite direction; no augmented leaps, no leaps of a seventh.
The penultimate bar makes a cadence: a sixth expanding to an octave (counterpoint above) or a third contracting to a unison (below), with the leading tone (raised in minor modes) moving to the final.
The line should have one climax (highest note), and not outline a tritone.

widget.title: A first-species example in D Dorian (cantus below, counterpoint above)

blocks.text: (Check the intervals: 5, 3, 6, 6, 3, 6, 3, 3, 3, 6, 8. One climax (D5), contrary motion into the final octave, and the raised C♯ as leading tone.)

items: Second species: two notes against one. The first of each pair must be consonant; the second may be a dissonant passing tone.
Third species: four notes against one. Adds neighbour tones and figures like the cambiata (a stepwise dissonance left by a leap of a third).

Fourth species: syncopated, the counterpoint tied across the bar line. Teaches suspensions: a consonance prepared on the weak beat becomes a dissonance on the strong beat and resolves down by step (7–6, 4–3 above the cantus; 2–3 below).
Fifth species (florid): a free mixture of the other four, with some decoration. This is where counterpoint starts to sound like real music.

blocks.text: Play two-voice counterpoint with one voice in each hand, then sing one line while playing the other. Bach's Two-Part Inventions are the classic keyboard study: each is a short piece in which two equal lines imitate and answer one another.

items: Imitation, Canon and Fugue (#/arts/music-theory/counterpoint/imitation-and-fugue): counterpoint where the voices share material.

blocks.title: Check the intervals
blocks.text: Over a cantus C4–D4–E4–D4–C4, a counterpoint above sings G4–F4–C5–B4–C5. Check it against the first-species rules.
solution: Intervals: C–G P5, D–F m3, E–C m6, D–B M6, C–C P8. All consonant, beginning and ending on perfect consonances.
Motion: the octave at the end is approached in contrary motion (B4 up to C5, D4 down to C4), a correct 6–8 cadence with the leading tone rising. No parallel fifths or octaves.
Melody: the leap F4–C5 (up a fifth) is followed by a step down, as it should be; the climax C5 is reached twice, a small weakness.
blocks.answer: It is correct; at most, the repeated climax is a stylistic weakness

blocks.title: Parallels
blocks.text: Two voices move from D–A (a fifth) to E–B. Which kind of motion, and is it allowed?
solution: Both move up a step and keep a perfect fifth: parallel fifths, forbidden in strict counterpoint.
